book.title: Competing Against Luck: The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice
book.author: Clayton M. Christensen, Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon, David S. Duncan

chapterBreakdown.gentle: Once you stop staring only at the product, the next question is what the buyer is really trying to move toward. This chapter calls that movement progress. A product can describe what someone bought, but it cannot explain what better state the person was trying to reach. That is why the same person can choose different answers in different moments without being inconsistent. The active progress target changed. Sometimes the progress is practical, like saving time or avoiding hassle. Sometimes it also includes social or emotional pressure, like wanting to feel responsible, calm, or in control. Those layers matter only when they stay tied to a real situation. If you leave the situation out, progress turns vague. If you keep the situation visible, the product makes more sense because you can see what kind of movement the buyer was trying to hire.
chapterBreakdown.direct: A buying moment gets clearer once you ask what the person is actually trying to change. This chapter answers with progress. People do not choose products only for attributes. They hire them to move from an unsatisfying state to a better one in specific circumstances. Products are too thin to carry that explanation alone. The progress may be functional, social, and emotional at the same time. A buyer might want less hassle, more confidence, or relief from a tense situation, all in one choice. The key is that those forces do not float in abstraction. They come from the circumstances. Progress is therefore a better test than product labels or buyer stereotypes. Once progress is clear, the product can be judged more honestly because the team is no longer guessing at a category average. It is asking whether the offering helps the person make the movement the situation actually demands.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: Products are easy to see, which is exactly why they are a weak place to stop. The deeper question is what progress the buyer is trying to make. That is the real target. A product names the object. Progress names the movement the person wants badly enough to hire an answer. The movement is not only practical. It can also carry social pressure and emotional relief, but only inside a real situation. Strip the circumstance away and progress becomes mush. Keep it visible and the job gets sharper. The same person can hire different answers on different days because the progress battle changed. That is not inconsistency. It is evidence that the moment, not the profile, is doing the explanatory work. It also explains why a technically decent answer can still lose if it misses the state the buyer is desperate to reach.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
A buyer can choose the same kind of product on two different days and still be trying to make two different kinds of progress. That is the pressure this chapter names clearly. Progress means the movement from one condition to a better one in a particular circumstance. Product language alone stays too thin because it can tell you what was bought, but not what kind of change the buyer hoped to create. It can list the item while missing the movement.

This matters because the desired change is rarely only practical. A product may save time, reduce hassle, avoid a mess, lower anxiety, or help a person feel competent in front of other people. The chapter's point is not that every purchase is secretly dramatic. It is that a hiring decision can carry functional, social, and emotional pressure at the same time. If a team studies only the practical layer, it will miss part of the reason the answer felt right.

The chapter also protects itself from turning sentimental. The emotional or social layer matters only when it stays connected to a concrete situation. A commuter wants more than calories during a long drive, but that extra meaning still comes from the drive itself. A parent wants more than convenience during a tense stop with a child, but the feeling of calm is still tied to that particular moment. The situation keeps progress from turning into a vague wish.

A buyer can therefore look inconsistent under a product lens and coherent under a progress lens. One moment activates a convenience problem. Another activates reassurance, status, relief, or control. The person did not change identity. The active progress target changed. The movement, not the profile, is doing the explanatory work.

The practical payoff is cleaner judgment. Once a team can name the progress at stake, it can evaluate the offering against a stronger standard: does this product help the person make the movement the circumstance is demanding, or is it only adding attributes to a category shell?
chapterBreakdown.direct:
A buying moment becomes easier to explain once the team stops asking what product won and starts asking what change the buyer was trying to achieve. The answer this chapter gives is progress. A customer is trying to move from an unsatisfying state to a better one, and that movement gives the job its shape.

Products are weak explanatory units for that reason. A product describes the object exchanged. Progress describes the change the buyer is trying to achieve. The difference is not cosmetic. It changes what a team listens for. Instead of collecting opinions about features, the team starts asking what practical result, emotional relief, or social outcome would make the situation feel better enough to justify the hire. It also changes what counts as a good competitor, because the real rival is any answer that helps create that better state.

The chapter's next move is important. Progress is not only functional. Buyers may also want to feel responsible, calm, capable, accepted, or less exposed. Those social and emotional forces are not extra decoration around the real job. They are often part of the job itself. A practical fix that ignores those forces may look good on paper and still lose in the market.

The chapter also draws a limit. Progress cannot become a vague synonym for aspiration. It has to stay tied to a circumstance. If the team says the buyer wants a better life, clearer confidence, or more freedom, the explanation is probably too broad to guide design. Progress becomes useful only when it names a movement that a real situation makes urgent. That is what keeps the theory operational rather than flattering.

This is also how the framework explains changing behavior. The same person may hire one solution in one context and a different one in another because the active progress target has shifted. That is not irrationality. It is situational coherence. Once that is clear, product design and messaging can be judged against the actual movement the buyer is trying to make instead of against an average persona story.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A product can look sharp on paper and still fail because the buyer was never hiring the object for its own sake. The real target is progress. A buyer is trying to move from one state to a better one, and that desired movement is what gives the decision real shape.

Product talk runs out fast for that reason. It can describe attributes, but it cannot tell you what better looks like from inside the buyer's situation. Progress can. It names the change the person is chasing hard enough to spend money, attention, and risk to get there.

The chapter also refuses the lazy version of this idea. Progress is not just practical utility, and it is not just a mood either. It can include functional, social, and emotional pressure in one hire. A person may want less hassle, less embarrassment, more control, or a cleaner signal about who they are in the moment. If a team strips the choice down to features alone, it can miss the force that actually made the answer win.

At the same time, the theory goes soft if those forces float free of the situation. Once progress becomes generic self-improvement language, the chapter loses its teeth. The only progress that matters here is the kind a real circumstance makes urgent enough to organize a choice. That pressure is what keeps the theory closer to causality than to branding.

That limit explains why behavior that looks inconsistent under a product lens often becomes clear under a progress lens. The same person can hire different answers across different situations because the demanded movement changed. The profile did not fail. It was never carrying the decision logic well enough to begin with.

This chapter sharpens innovation work by giving teams a better test. Do not ask whether the product sounds attractive in the category. Ask whether it helps the buyer make the right movement under the actual pressure of the moment. That is the point where features stop being guesses and start being judged against something real.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The opening chapter made one decisive move: stop treating the product category as the center of demand. This chapter asks what should replace it. The answer is progress. A buyer is trying to move from one state to a better one in a particular circumstance, and that movement gives the job its real content. Without that movement, the product remains a description of what was bought rather than an explanation of why it won.

This matters because a better state is rarely only practical. A person may want speed, less mess, lower risk, more confidence, a cleaner social signal, or relief from a small tension that has built up in the moment. The chapter's force comes from insisting that functional, social, and emotional pressure can all be part of the same hire. The layers are not interchangeable, but they can be active together.

That is also why a product can look rational on paper and still fail in the market. If a team clears the functional problem but ignores the social or emotional pressure, the answer may still feel wrong to the buyer. A parent may not only want a snack that works. The parent may want a moment that stays calm. A student may not only want a program with the right courses. The student may want a path that feels responsible and legible to other people. The practical layer matters, but it does not always close the decision.

The chapter stays disciplined by refusing to let those extra layers drift into general human truth. Social and emotional pressure matters here only when it is tied to a situation. That tie is what keeps the theory causal. Once progress is described too broadly, the concept becomes a mood board instead of an explanation. A demand story like "I want a better life" cannot guide design. A story like "I need a cleaner, calmer answer in this exact moment" can.

This gives the framework a useful contradiction. Progress has to be richer than features or demographics, or it cannot explain enough. But it also has to stay narrower than aspiration language, or it explains too little. The chapter works in that narrow band. Progress must be broad enough to include practical, social, and emotional movement, yet specific enough to remain anchored to the situation that made the hire urgent.

That tension also clarifies apparent inconsistency in behavior. Under a product lens, one person may look fickle. Under a progress lens, the same person can look coherent across changing situations. The identity did not shift. The active movement did. Once the moment changes, the standard for a good answer changes with it.

The payoff is operational rather than poetic. Teams can ask better questions once progress becomes the target. What movement is the buyer trying to make? Which pressure layers are active in that movement? What friction in the old state makes the hire necessary now? Those questions are strong because they stay close to action while reaching deeper than attributes. The next chapter needs to show that this is not just a careful reinterpretation of the milkshake story, but a theory that travels across settings in the wild.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
A buyer can look predictable on a spreadsheet and still remain badly explained until you name the movement the person is trying to make. That is the problem this chapter solves with progress. If the category label is too blunt and the product itself is too static, the team needs a better unit of analysis. Progress gives the job coherence because it names the desired change.

Product descriptions cannot carry enough causal weight for that task. They can tell you what was purchased, but not what better looked like from inside the buyer's moment. Progress does. It captures the change the person is trying to achieve and therefore gives the team a stronger basis for research, design, and competition. It also keeps research closer to causality because the team starts with change sought under pressure instead of traits listed after the fact.

The chapter deepens the model by refusing a purely functional account. Buyers may want speed, simplicity, and lower effort, but they may also want to feel responsible, competent, calm, accepted, or less exposed. Those social and emotional forces are not ornamental. In many cases they help determine whether the practical answer feels complete enough to hire. That means a team cannot stop with utility and still assume the explanation is finished.

That creates a real design discipline. A team can build something that solves the task and still fail because the answer mishandles the buyer's social or emotional stakes. The product might work technically while failing situationally. The chapter does more than add empathy language. It expands what counts as part of the job. That expansion matters because many weak products solve the visible task while leaving the hidden tension alive for buyers.

The chapter also sets a limit on itself. Progress cannot become a vague synonym for self-improvement or aspiration. If the explanation drifts that far, it loses operational value. Progress is only useful when it stays attached to the circumstance that makes a particular movement urgent enough to organize a choice.

This gives the framework a narrow but powerful center. It must be wider than feature logic so it can include the full pressure of the moment, and narrower than generic life language so it can still guide decisions. That balance explains why the same buyer can make different choices across different contexts without becoming analytically mysterious. The active progress target changed, so the required answer changed too. The theory gets stronger, not weaker, when it can explain those shifts without calling them random. It keeps coherence where surface behavior looked messy.

The chapter's payoff is practical. Once progress becomes the target, teams can test whether an offering helps the buyer move in the needed way, whether it addresses all active pressure layers, and whether the message fits the real urgency of the moment. The next chapter has to prove that this frame travels beyond one or two illustrative cases and holds across categories in the wild.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A buyer can reward a product on Monday and ignore it on Thursday without becoming irrational. The movement changed. That is the reality this chapter forces into the center. If you actually want a theory of demand instead of prettier research notes, category language has to give way to progress.

That is already stronger than product talk because the product only names the object. Progress names the change the person is chasing hard enough to act on. Without that change, the category stays descriptive and demand stays blurry. The real question becomes what better state was urgent enough to command money, attention, and risk.

The chapter gets tougher when it refuses the comfort of a purely functional answer. Buyers do not only want utility. They may also want relief, control, reassurance, legitimacy, or a cleaner social position inside the moment. Those forces are not decorative. They can decide whether the practical answer feels complete enough to choose.

This is where weak teams lose. They solve the task and miss the stakes. They reduce the choice to utility while the buyer is also managing embarrassment, identity, or a need for calm. Then they act surprised when a technically solid product loses to a messier competitor that fits the moment better. The hidden loss is that the team starts trusting feature logic even more after the miss.

The chapter stays honest by drawing a hard boundary. Progress cannot float free of the circumstance. The second it turns into broad aspiration language, it stops guiding design and starts flattering the team. Useful progress is situational, pressured, and specific enough to separate a live hire from generic desire. That discipline is what keeps the theory closer to demand than to storytelling theater.

That creates the chapter's real tension. Progress has to be richer than features or demographics, or it misses too much. But it also has to stay tighter than vague self-improvement rhetoric, or it explains nothing worth building against. The theory only works in that disciplined middle band. That middle band is why the framework can stay concrete while still reaching below surface features. It is also why the chapter can deepen demand logic without turning mystical.

Hold that line and messy behavior starts reading differently. The same person can hire different answers because the demanded movement changed with the scene, the pressure mix, and the standard for what counts as enough. Different stakes activate different competitors, different sacrifices, and different definitions of relief. The profile did not fail. The profile was never carrying the decision logic hard enough to begin with.

That is the upgrade this chapter offers. It gives teams a harder test than product appeal. Ask what movement the buyer needs, what pressures are packed inside it, and whether the offering actually helps the person get there under the conditions that make the choice urgent. The next chapter has to show that this frame survives contact with many settings, not just the opening examples.

examples.title: Lila Rewrites the Feature Request as a Progress Question

scenario.gentle: Lila is reviewing survey responses for a budgeting app. Users keep asking for more colorful charts, but the comments also mention feeling overwhelmed every Sunday night when bills pile up.
scenario.direct: Lila's dashboard is full of requested features. The strongest signal, though, is that users feel tense and behind before the charts even matter.
scenario.competitive: The team wants to ship prettier charts. Lila can either obey the feature noise or ask what movement users are actually paying for on Sunday night.

whatToDo.gentle: Reframe the discussion around the better state users are trying to reach. Ask whether the app is helping them feel clearer and more in control before adding another chart style.
whatToDo.direct: Pull the team off the feature list and define the progress target in the moment of use: less confusion, more control, lower stress.
whatToDo.competitive: Drop the color debate. Force the room to name the movement worth hiring before it ships decoration.

whyItMatters.gentle: The product gets judged more honestly once the team knows what better is supposed to feel like in that situation.
whyItMatters.direct: Progress gives the team a stronger test than popularity of requests alone.
whyItMatters.competitive: Without the movement, features are just polished guesses.

examples.title: Omar Hears That the Program Choice Is About More Than the Course List

scenario.gentle: Omar meets Ms. Chen in the advising office with two program sheets spread across the desk. He keeps comparing course lists, but he also keeps saying he wants to feel sure he is not wasting time.
scenario.direct: Omar talks as if he is choosing between classes, yet the real pressure in the room is whether his decision will feel responsible and safe enough to commit to.
scenario.competitive: Omar thinks he is buying a course path. Ms. Chen can see he is really trying to buy progress toward certainty.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask what better state Omar wants this decision to create, not only which courses look useful. Keep the practical and emotional pressures in the same conversation.
whatToDo.direct: Define the progress target before comparing the program options. Is he buying skills, confidence, legitimacy, or some combination of all three?
whatToDo.competitive: Stop treating the course sheet as the whole decision. Name the movement the choice is supposed to secure.

whyItMatters.gentle: A better decision appears when the practical path and the feeling of responsible progress are examined together.
whyItMatters.direct: The social and emotional stakes are part of the job, not noise around it.
whyItMatters.competitive: Ignore the real movement and the course list will keep lying about what matters.

examples.title: Hannah Notices the Same Tool Is Serving Convenience in One Moment and Reassurance in Another

scenario.gentle: Hannah keeps using the same meal-delivery app. On work nights she uses it to avoid hassle. On weekends she uses it when she feels too drained to plan and wants the relief of not deciding.
scenario.direct: The app looks like one product habit, but Hannah realizes one moment is about convenience and another is about emotional relief.
scenario.competitive: Hannah thought she was loyal to the app. She is really hiring it for two different movements.

whatToDo.gentle: Write down the two situations separately and identify what better state each one is supposed to create.
whatToDo.direct: Split the convenience job from the reassurance job before deciding whether the app is still the best answer in both cases.
whatToDo.competitive: Separate the movements or you will keep treating one habit as one demand story.

whyItMatters.gentle: One product can feel reliable for different reasons in different moments.
whyItMatters.direct: The multidimensional job becomes clearer once the situations are pulled apart.
whyItMatters.competitive: Same app, different pressure, different standard.

examples.title: Victor's Postmortem Shows That the Team Solved the Task but Missed the Tension

scenario.gentle: Victor reviews a failed onboarding flow for a software tool. The screens were efficient, but new users kept abandoning the process halfway through profile setup.
scenario.direct: The product team reduced clicks and improved speed, yet users still dropped out when the setup started feeling exposing and confusing.
scenario.competitive: Victor's team solved the task and still lost the hire. The missing layer was not another field. It was the pressure users felt while moving through the flow.

whatToDo.gentle: Revisit the onboarding moment and ask what functional, social, and emotional pressures are active while users set up the tool.
whatToDo.direct: Audit the abandoned flow for more than efficiency. Identify where confusion, exposure, or self-doubt are still blocking progress.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop congratulating the click reduction. Diagnose the pressure the flow still leaves alive.

whyItMatters.gentle: A technically smoother product can still fail if the real movement is not fully supported.
whyItMatters.direct: The example transfers the chapter beyond consumer goods into software design and adoption.
whyItMatters.competitive: Utility alone does not win if the moment still feels wrong.

examples.title: Ava Predicts One Reason Students Buy the Bag and Then Sees Three Layers of Progress

scenario.gentle: Ava helps stock a campus store and assumes students buy one laptop bag mainly for extra space. Then she starts hearing comments about looking professional for presentations and feeling less scattered during heavy days.
scenario.direct: Ava expected the bag to win on utility alone. Observation reveals practical convenience, social signal, and emotional relief all working at once.
scenario.competitive: Ava thought the bag sold on pockets. The buyers are also hiring calm and credibility.

whatToDo.gentle: Separate what the bag does physically from what better state it helps students reach during demanding days.
whatToDo.direct: Map the practical, social, and emotional movement the bag is serving before changing the assortment.
whatToDo.competitive: Do not reduce a layered hire to storage capacity. Name the whole movement.

whyItMatters.gentle: The common trap is assuming the visible feature is the whole explanation.
whyItMatters.direct: Progress often contains more than the task the product obviously performs.
whyItMatters.competitive: Visible utility is often only the front half of the hire.

examples.title: Lucas Stops Shopping by Specs Once He Names the Better State He Wants

scenario.gentle: Before, Lucas compared headphones only by battery life and sound quality. After a week of noticing when he actually used them, he realized he mainly wanted to feel less interrupted during noisy commutes and shared workspaces.
scenario.direct: Lucas moved from spec comparison to progress comparison once he saw the moments where the headphones mattered most.
scenario.competitive: Lucas stopped shopping for hardware and started shopping for a better state.

whatToDo.gentle: Name the movement you want first, then compare products against whether they create that state in the moments that matter.
whatToDo.direct: Let the progress target reset the decision criteria before you compare attributes.
whatToDo.competitive: Shop against the movement, not against the spec sheet.

explanation.gentle: A single job can contain practical, social, and emotional pressure together.
explanation.direct: The chapter explicitly expands the job beyond function alone to include social and emotional stakes.
explanation.competitive: One hire can clear the task and the feeling around it.

questions.prompt: A team knows users want faster setup, but many still quit midway because the flow feels exposing. What is the chapter's best reading?
choices: The team solved the practical task but missed another active pressure layer
The users probably misunderstood the instructions
The team should ignore emotional feedback and improve speed even more

explanation.gentle: A technically smoother path can still fail if the emotional or social pressure in the moment stays alive.
explanation.direct: This is exactly the chapter's warning. Function alone may not complete the hire.
explanation.competitive: They cleared clicks and left the tension untouched.

questions.prompt: Lila's team keeps debating a new app feature. Which move fits the chapter best?
choices: Ask which competing app has the nicest version of that feature
Define the better state users are trying to reach in the exact moment they open the app
Wait for more survey percentages before changing the roadmap

explanation.gentle: The chapter pushes the team toward the progress target before another feature debate begins.
explanation.direct: Choice B restores the movement the product is supposed to create under the real circumstance.
explanation.competitive: That move forces the room to answer the hire instead of admiring the object.

questions.prompt: Why can a buyer look inconsistent under a product lens but coherent under a progress lens?
choices: Because product quality changes randomly from day to day
Because the active progress target can shift across different situations
Because buyers usually lie when they describe what they want

explanation.gentle: The person may be facing different struggles in different moments. That changes what a good answer looks like.
explanation.direct: The chapter explains variation through changing circumstances, not through buyer irrationality.
explanation.competitive: Different movement, different hire. That is coherence, not chaos.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's limit on progress language?
choices: Progress should describe whatever long-term aspiration sounds inspiring
Progress only matters when it is tied to the situation making the choice urgent
Progress should ignore emotional stakes so it stays objective

explanation.gentle: The idea stays useful only when the movement is attached to a real circumstance.
explanation.direct: Progress becomes vague and weak if it drifts into broad aspiration language.

questions.prompt: Omar is choosing between two academic programs. What would this chapter say he should clarify first?
choices: Which program has the longer course list
Which program aligns with the better state he is trying to reach in this decision
Which program is more popular with his friends

explanation.gentle: The chapter pushes beyond the visible options to the movement the choice is supposed to create.
explanation.direct: Course lists matter, but the decisive frame is the progress Omar needs this decision to deliver.
explanation.competitive: If he cannot name the movement, the program sheets will keep distracting him.

questions.prompt: Hannah uses the same delivery app on work nights for convenience and on drained weekends for reassurance. What does that show?
choices: She should stop using the app because her preferences are unstable
The app is serving more than one progress target across different moments
Convenience and reassurance are really the same motive

explanation.gentle: The same product can serve different forms of progress in different situations.
explanation.direct: This is a good example of one object supporting more than one active job across contexts.

questions.prompt: Which statement best shows progress language going weak?
choices: Our users want a calmer setup flow when they first create an account in a rushed environment
Our users want to feel better about life in general
Our users want less confusion and less exposure while they enter sensitive information

explanation.gentle: The middle option is too broad to guide a real design choice because it is detached from a specific situation.
explanation.direct: That statement fails the chapter's test. It names aspiration without enough circumstance to stay operational.
explanation.competitive: That is flattering fog, not usable progress.

questions.prompt: If this chapter is right, what does the book need to prove next?
choices: That one category can contain infinite emotional interpretations
That the progress frame can explain choices across many settings in the wild
That demographics no longer matter for any business decision

explanation.gentle: The next step is to show the theory working beyond the opening examples.
explanation.direct: This chapter sets up a broader test. The frame now has to travel across categories and contexts.
explanation.competitive: A real theory has to survive outside the neat first cases.

coreSkill.gentle: The core skill is naming the better state a person wants from a specific moment before comparing products.
coreSkill.direct: This chapter teaches progress diagnosis: define the movement the circumstance makes urgent and test answers against it.
coreSkill.competitive: The skill is reading the movement before you admire the object.

plan.gentle: If a roadmap discussion turns into feature comparison, then ask what better state the user is trying to reach in that moment.
plan.direct: If the team is stuck on attributes, then define the movement, the active pressure layers, and the old friction first.
plan.competitive: If the room is arguing features, force it to name the movement or keep guessing.

plan.gentle: If a school choice feels harder than the visible options suggest, then write down the practical, social, and emotional movement you want from the decision.
plan.direct: If one academic or campus decision feels tangled, then separate what result, what social signal, and what emotional relief you want it to create.
plan.competitive: If the decision sheet looks clear but you still feel stuck, identify the movement the paper is missing.

plan.gentle: If the same product feels useful for different reasons across the week, then split the situations and name the progress each one is serving.
plan.direct: If a repeat purchase seems inconsistent, then compare the active movement in each circumstance before judging the product.
plan.competitive: If one habit feels like two stories, split the movements before you buy again.

twentyFourHourChallenge.gentle: In the next 24 hours, write down one recent choice and name the better state you wanted from that exact moment.
twentyFourHourChallenge.direct: Within a day, take one purchase and list the functional, social, and emotional pressures that were active in it.
twentyFourHourChallenge.competitive: Before tomorrow ends, catch one hire and state the movement it had to deliver.

weeklyPractice.gentle: Once this week, compare two moments where you used the same product and ask whether the progress target was actually the same.
weeklyPractice.direct: Run one weekly progress audit by checking whether one repeated product is serving different movements across different situations.
weeklyPractice.competitive: This week, test one habit for hidden shifts in the movement you keep paying it to win.

front.gentle: What replaces the product as the explanatory center?
front.direct: What does the buyer really hire here?

back.direct: The movement the buyer wants to make.

front.gentle: Which three pressure layers can one job include?
front.direct: What dimensions can be active together in a hire?
front.competitive: What stack can one movement carry?

front.gentle: Why is circumstance necessary when naming progress?
front.competitive: What stops progress from turning soft?

back.gentle: The real situation that makes the movement urgent.
back.direct: Circumstance keeps the movement specific enough to guide choices.

front.gentle: Why can one person hire different answers without being inconsistent?
front.direct: What changes when behavior shifts coherently across contexts?
front.competitive: What actually changed when the hire changed?

front.gentle: Finish the test: a good offering helps the buyer...
front.direct: What should a product be judged against?
front.competitive: What is the hard standard here?

back.gentle: Make the needed movement in that moment.
back.direct: Move toward the better state the situation demands.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: A job is really the progress a person wants to make in a specific moment. Products matter, but they become clearer only after the movement, the pressure, and the situation are named.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: Progress becomes the better explanatory unit because it captures the desired change inside the circumstance, including functional, social, and emotional pressure.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: Products describe what sold. Progress explains why it was worth hiring. If you miss the movement, you keep building against a category shell.
